title: try / catch / finally
definition: A syntax structure that allows you to execute code that might fail (`try`), gracefully handle the error if it does fail (`catch`), and execute cleanup code regardless of the outcome (`finally`).
simpleExplanation: Try: 'Hey JS, try to do this risky thing.' Catch: 'If it explodes, don't crash the whole app, just run this backup plan.' Finally: 'No matter if it exploded or succeeded, clean up your mess.'
realWorldExample: Trying to parse a JSON string from LocalStorage. If the string is corrupted, `JSON.parse` will throw an error. Wrapping it in a try/catch prevents the app from white-screening.

basic: What happens if an error occurs inside the `try` block?
advanced: Can a `try/catch` block catch errors inside a `setTimeout` callback?

answers.question: Is finally mandatory?
answers.answer: No. You can have just `try/catch`, or just `try/finally` (which runs the cleanup but doesn't suppress the crash). You rarely use `finally` in frontend JS, but it is heavily used in Node.js to close database/file streams.

answers.question: Can try/catch catch setTimeout errors?
answers.answer: NO! `try/catch` is completely synchronous. The `try` block finishes instantly, and 1 second later the `setTimeout` callback throws an error. The `catch` block has already finished and packed up its bags. The error will crash the app. You must put the `try/catch` INSIDE the setTimeout callback.
